segments.text: There you go. There you go. Good job. Good job. Hilary: Bryan Johnson, the tech entrepreneur who sold Venmo for $800 million, has spent a fortune on a quest to stay young forever. "Don't die" is the general theme of what we're trying to do.

It's humanity's only objective. Hilary: He's been open about spending an average of $2 million a year on some of the world's most exclusive health treatments. We definitely have rejected modern society's approach on food. So yeah, it is a pharmacy in here.

Hilary: Some scientists have called his goals unachievable and his methods risky. They didn't know what to call me, like a tech bro or a biohacker. They would be like, "That's a crazy, eccentric billionaire." And I wanted to say, just like you view LeBron James, who spends a lot of money on his body, when he performs well on the court, we say, "Good job, LeBron." When someone else spends money on their health and wellness, you want to dunk on them.

And I wanted to change the perception that I am a professional rejuvenation athlete. We wanted to understand what's it really like and why is he doing it. So come with us now. We're going to go take a look. Oh my God, I feel like a bug. Now I want to know what's in Bryan Johnson's fridge.

Yeah, let's do it. OK. So what do we have in here? These are plasmalogens. This is a prescription. These are prescriptions. This is a microbiome product. These are my meals. So I have a chef that comes to the house once a week. And she prepares food for three or four days.

So this is my nutty pudding. So I eat a lot of broccoli, a lot of cauliflower. Actually, my fridge is like 50% therapies. And the other is like 50% vegetables and fruits. Hilary: Johnson's diet includes 70 pounds of vegetables each month.

He says he takes in about 1,977 calories a day. And every calorie must serve a purpose for his longevity goals. A lot of people perceive my endeavor to be like this crazy rich guy doing weird things. Actually, what we're doing is very practical.

So I was trying to become the healthiest person on planet Earth. And I couldn't do that unless I started testing all my foods. Today we're going to test 10 supermarket chocolates and determine how good or bad they are for you. Hilary: In September, Johnson said Blueprint, his longevity company that sells supplements, powdered drink mixes, and meals, spent $50,000 testing its foods for things like microplastics and heavy metals.

We both know that in society, it's very hard to be healthy. You go to work, you have to pass by 20 fast food places, there's snacks that are not good for you. We wanted to try to create a food protocol that made healthy decisions easy. Basically, we've taken the ingredients that have the highest potential for robustness in aging and made it in some easy, pleasant-to-consume format.

And so now with this dish, this is like a superfood superfood superfood. Because now you've got nuts, berries, proteins, chocolate, extra virgin olive oil, all sourced from some of the best in the entire world, in one dish.

Hilary: Johnson sells the pudding for $94 a pack, or about $3.31 per serving. I'm excited for you to taste it. It's almost like, almost like an oatmeal or something. Bryan: Yeah, and then one final thing is now add the 100% pure cocoa.

Hilary: OK. This is a generous amount of cocoa. Bryan: Yeah. So that's 6 grams a day. Hilary: I like it. Isn't that great? This is like your dinner? Yeah. So, at the dinners, I serve this because it usually is a crowd favorite. Hilary: In an effort to reduce his biological age and get better sleep, Johnson abides by a rather unconventional eating schedule.

His last meal of the day is around 11 a.m. This is a morning drink. This is Blueprint Longevity Mix, and it has 20 capsules into one drink. This is what you drink before you eat anything else? First thing in the morning. It smells kind of like Tang. OK. It's not very sweet, but it's like kind of fruity.

What's the fruity flavor? Like berry? Blood orange. Hilary: It's designed to function kind of like a daily multivitamin. It contains more than 275% of the recommended daily vitamin C allowance for adults, plus magnesium and ashwagandha. All this to supposedly give you more energy, support a healthy metabolism, and aid recovery from daily stressors, like sports.

It costs $1.63 per serving. I feel like I'm still getting used to the taste, but it's not unpleasant. I personally love this drink. It's like one of my favorite moments every day. Hilary: We're here in Bryan Johnson's pantry.

There's some Snake Oil in here. Bryan: That's right. Hilary: Snake Oil is the tongue-in-cheek branding for Johnson's very first product, which he debuted in 2023. It's actually just extra virgin olive oil. A single bottle costs $35, roughly three times the price of similar options you'd find at the grocery store.

We're curious to know, you obviously are very famous for taking so many different supplements. Do you have a favorite like that you feel is like the best bang for the buck, or is that not really how the system works? It's really a bunch of things. It's really everything in its proper amount is the right way.

And so that's what we've tried to do. We just simply said, "What has the best evidence, and what will do the most good?" And then we just put it together. These are my exact pills. Hilary: Johnson says he takes more than 100 pills a day. He says this costs him around $11 each day, or more than $4,000 a year.

But experts say when it comes to supplements, more isn't necessarily better. Most longevity doctors recommend adding supplements to a person's routine one at a time, and then carefully measuring the effect, keeping a close eye on how each compound interacts with a person's diet, lifestyle, and medication, and whether it's actually showing some benefit.

Now, before we go up the stairs, the risk of falling on stairs is so significant. And if you fall, it can be the most detrimental thing to your lifespan. A nice test of biological age is how many steps you can take in any given moment and still maintain your balance.

So, typically, we take one step. You can extend to two, extend to three. But if you try three, then you have to, basically, extend a certain amount. You have to maintain balance and then avoiding using the guardrail. And so it gives people just a general intuition, like, how is their body doing.

Pretty impressive. I'm not going to lie. Let's try. OK, I guess I have to go for three, even though I feel like two is the safe... Yeah, so, if you want to be safe and do two, that's also just fine. I got long legs, though. Oh my gosh. This is not happening.

Bryan: Yeah. Two's good. Hilary: I'm so tempted by the three. There you go. There you go. Good job. Good job. Thank you. I feel my heart racing. Do you feel like your heart pound a little after that? Bryan: No. Hilary: Not at all. All right. Before you come into the clinic, you need to read a warning sign.

Hilary: "May cause loss of age"? That's right. So just be aware that that is a risk. So we try to be like a full medical-grade clinic. We just want to use data and science. And so everything you see in here is either measuring something or doing a therapy.

This measures the biological age of skin. This is skin rejuvenation. This is whole-body measurement with ultrasound. This is cold air, which is like an anesthesia, when we do things on the face that are very painful. This is electromagnetic therapy to, basically, do 20,000 situps in 30 minutes.

That's red light therapy. And then in the closet over there, we have all the supplies to do blood draw, blood spinnage, a whole bunch of other therapies. Hilary: These are all medical devices. Some are used to diagnose health conditions, others treat sports injuries and aid with rehab, or are used postpartum.

But they're not generally used as preventative care tools, the way Bryan is using them here. So, for example, this is medical-grade ultrasound. A lot of people are familiar with that looking at babies in the womb. But you can also use ultrasound looking at the entire body, all of your joints, the pancreas, the hips, the bladder, the brain, the lungs, the heart.

So we routinely measure my body with ultrasound. Hilary: This is a portable ultrasound machine and generally costs anywhere from $15,000 to $40,000. Physicians say this is a great basic tool, but it's not something people need to use all the time and not necessarily that useful for improving longevity.

This device is a skin therapy. So it helps increase elastin and collagen. So, as you age, you lose collagen and you lose elastin, which means the skin sags and wrinkles. So you're trying to combat those effects with this therapy.

Experts say this kind of radio-frequency skin therapy is kind of like a facelift without the surgery, firming and lifting sagging skin by triggering production of new skin cells through heat. Because the device makes your skin hot, there is a risk of redness, swelling, and even burning.

Do you put this wand on your face? So yeah, this one is for the body. So, this actually gets rid of excess fat. Hilary: Oh, wow. Whereas this one is a face applicator where you have a much smaller focal point. Hilary: Oh, interesting.

It's called ultrasonic cavitation. And the machine is supposed to break apart fat deposits under the skin using ultrasound frequencies. It's supposed to be like a non-invasive liposuction, but studies on how well it actually works are still mixed. And then this is a professional hearing grade system. So I have hearing loss in my left ear equal to a 64-year-old.

So, from 4,000 hertz to 12,000 hertz, I'm basically deaf. And so I miss out on so much of life's experiences because I can't hear in that range. Now, I can hear a conversation, I can hear music, but there are specific sounds in those ranges. So we've been trying very hard to restore hearing with no success.

So, some success in doing some things in the body. Other things we just have not succeeded at. We bought these panels for $600 per panel. Hilary: OK. So, very affordable. So if you want to try this. Hilary: Yeah. OK, so you can just step in here, watch your feet as you step in, and just want to be equal distance from both.

Hilary: OK. And how often do you do this? Daily. It's wonderful. It's soothing. All right. I'm going to put on these glasses. Oh my god, I feel like a bug. I can't see a thing. OK, so I'm now going to turn the lights on. Hilary: OK. And so I'm going to do four.
One. Hilary: Wow. Two. Three. Four. Hilary: Oh, it's super warm. And how long do you spend in here?

Bryan: Roughly, three to six minutes a day. Hilary: OK. Bryan: And so I'll do frontal facing, and then I'll turn and do side facing. And it helps with recovery. It helps with energy. There's even clinical studies to show it helps on mood.

So it's really multifaceted and just generally a good health practice. And I've heard it's good for wound healing. Bryan: That's correct. Doing it daily is a really nice complement after working out. Hilary: Yeah. Almost feels like a sauna. Bryan: Yes.

Hilary: Red light therapy is a real technique that's used for wound healing. But Bryan's machine here probably isn't very effective. Experts say your skin should not heat up. The objective is whole-body wellness. And so now I think you're starting to get an idea, like if you were to spend a day with me, and we were to eat all the foods we have and exercise and do these therapies, you could see how it'd be possible you'd feel better.

So this is why I've never felt better in my entire life. I've never felt more stable. I've never been less affected by stress or by insult. I'm just good with everything. And that wasn't the case before. It was a very emotionally rocky and turbulent life.

Hilary: Johnson has also invested in upgrades to a $6.8 million home to achieve his longevity goals. He installed UV filters on his windows, put an air purification device in every room, and he has the filtered water tested on a routine basis. Bryan: This is my happy place.

So one hour every day I spend in the gym doing a variety of exercises, maybe over 40. So a lot of people focus in the gym, like building big muscles. And I'm trying to be fast. I'm trying to be flexible. I'm trying to be able to do everything I can in life.

Get up the stairs. Exactly. So just like if my kids want to play a game of basketball, I can play it. If we want to race, I can race. If I want to jump high, I can jump high. So I'm really trying to maintain ability. And so I'll give you a couple of examples. Hilary: Yeah. Bryan: Like if you want to come over here.

Hilary: OK. And you want to put your feet here. So you have toes at the end, and then just come down and do a deep squat all the way down. Hilary: Oh, wow. Yep. And then come back up. So try to keep your hips straight, and then you go all the way down and try to get your knees.

Sit down as far as you can. OK. I think that's as far as I can. Yeah. Then come back up, and then push the pelvis forward. There you go. And then go down again. All the way down, as far as you can. Let me watch you do it one more time. Have your hamstrings touching. So when you go down, just fully sit.

So these are like... There's no space in between... Hilary: Yeah. the hamstrings. You're just fully seated down. Hilary: OK. So a deep, deep squat. Oh, yeah. See, I got to work on my - Yeah. Which is totally expected, because you're doing things you don't do on a daily basis.

So, totally natural. I just do a lot of things that focus on my flexibility and my range of motion throughout the gym. So I'm showing you things that are hard. Hilary: OK. Just to highlight. So we spend the majority of our time in a seated position. We're at our desks, and so our muscles here get pretty tight.

And so if you were to stretch these muscles, this is called a couch stretch. You have this leg here and this leg back, and you have this leg up against the wall. So, a straight 90. And you can go forward and stretch it and just straight up here, but you feel this stretch through here.

Hilary: Oh, yeah. So if you want to try that. OK. So, like that? Oh my gosh. You make it look so easy. Yeah. Just slow step your way into this. So in time, what you'd want to do is push this knee all the way back to the wall. But don't push it too hard.

Then, as you get more flexible, you can go back even further, straighten it, and then go all the way back. Yeah. I mean, I don't even need to move. I feel it already. I understand now why you beat me on the stairs. Bryan: (laughing) Yeah. Hilary: One hundred percent.
I think a lot of people are maybe confused or curious about what I do. So, "Don't die" is the general theme of what we're trying to do. What I'm proposing is the next major ideology of the world.
